chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'A man bequeathed to me (to be an executor), so I asked that he should associate with me a near relative of his. So he did it, and he, the one who bequeathed to me, mentioned that for him with the one who is an associate with regards to the bequest, are one hundred and fifty Dirhams as security, a bowl of silver. So when the man died, the executor said that he has a claim against him (the deceased) a certain measurements of wheat.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he establishes the evidence, otherwise there is nothing for him.'
I said to him, 'Is it permissible for him that he takes anything from what is in his hands?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not permissible for him.'

I said, 'What is your view, if that man is inimical towards him, so he takes his wealth, and he is able to take from his wealth what he takes, that would be for him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'This (situation) is not similar to this.'
ai.seo_question: Can an executor deduct their own debt from a security deposit held for the deceased without evidence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'holding in trust' (istid'af) versus 'right of retention' (haqq al-qabd), establishing that an executor cannot unilaterally convert a security deposit into payment for an unproven debt. The Imam distinguishes this legal retention from forcible seizure by an enemy, emphasizing that while force bypasses procedural proof, contractual or fiduciary retention requires valid evidence to justify appropriating the asset.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Fazal, from Ali Bin Uqba, from Bureyd Bin Muawiya, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘

I said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘A man bequeathed to me (to be an executor), so I asked that he should associate (someone else) with me who is a near relative of his. So he did it, and he, the one who bequeathed to me, mentioned that for him with the one who is an associate with regards to the bequest, are one hundred and fifty Dirhams as security, a bowl of silver. So when the man died, the executor said that he has a claim against him (the deceased) a certain measurements of wheat.
He<sup>asws</sup> said: If he establishes the evidence, otherwise there is nothing for him’.
I said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Is it Permissible for him that he takes anything from what is in his hands?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘It is not Permissible for him’.

I said, ‘What is your<sup>asws</sup> view, if that man is inimical towards him, so he takes his wealth, and he is able to take from his wealth what he takes, that would be for him?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘This (situation) is not similar to this’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from ibn Faddal from Ali ibn ‘Uqbah from Burayd ibn Mu‘awiyah who has narrated the following: “

I once said to abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, that a man made a will in which he appointed me as executor of the will. I asked him to appoint one more person of his relatives with me and he did. The testator told me that with the other executor of the will he has a bowl of silver, which is worth one hundred fifty dirham as a security item. When he dies the other executor of the will said that the testator owes him several Kur (a certain unit of measurement) of wheat.
He (the Imam) said, ‘If he presents testimony he can have it, but not without testimony.’
I then asked, ‘Can he compensate from what is in his hand?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘It is not lawful for him.’
I then said, ‘If one due to animosity takes away one’s assets, then it becomes possible for him to compensate his loss from his assets: if he can do so.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘This is not like that.’”
